items.title: The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
items.why: Argues that generative drug-design pipelines should be judged on dose and exposure (PBPK simulation), not only on predicted potency and toxicity. This is a preprint accepted at a NeurIPS workshop, and the results cover only three PARP1-targeted pipelines.
items.takeaway: Of 60 shortlisted molecules, the authors report that seven fail to reach sufficient target exposure.

items.title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
items.by: Pourmirzaei, M.; Alqarghuli, S.; Chen, K.; Pourmirzaei, M.; Xu, D.
items.why: A ligand-aware benchmark for residue-level binding-site prediction that tests generalisation to ligands unseen in training, with control experiments using scrambled and mismatched SMILES. It is a bioRxiv preprint (v2) and has not been peer reviewed.
items.takeaway: On unseen ligands the best stage reaches a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338, and the control inputs lower performance.

items.title: Similar visual tuning conceals different recovery dynamics in a model of macaque V1
items.by: Xialei Huang, Qingyu Yan, Zheng Bian, Zhuo-Cheng Xiao
items.why: Uses deep-network surrogates of local spiking-neuron responses to make a V1 circuit model cheap to evaluate. The surrogate's derivatives allow stability and perturbation analysis. It is an unfamiliar scientific-ML topic, and the preprint is unreviewed and a model-only study.
items.takeaway: The authors report that different pathway strengths can give similar visual responses but different recovery dynamics.

items.title: Multimodal single-cell analyses reveal distinct fusion-regulated transcriptional programs in Ewing sarcoma
items.why: Only the title was retrievable (the page excerpt was a browser challenge), so check the abstract and methods at the source.

items.title: The paradox of diffusion distillation
items.why: A deep dive into why diffusion models need many sampling steps and how the main distillation families cut that number.
items.takeaway: Distilling from a teacher lowers training-loss variance compared with standard diffusion training, but trades it for bias.

items.title: Guidance: a cheat code for diffusion models
items.why: A clear derivation of classifier and classifier-free guidance from Bayes' rule, including why guidance trades diversity for conditioning strength. It is a useful foundation for conditional generative models, including conditional molecular and protein generators.
items.takeaway: Classifier-free guidance is a combination of conditional and unconditional scores, and a scale above 1 sharpens conditioning at the cost of diversity.

items.title: Naturally Occurring Equivariance in Neural Networks
items.why: An interpretability article by Chris Olah and colleagues showing that vision networks learn rotated, scaled, flipped and hue-shifted copies of the same feature. Their circuit analysis links these copies through symmetric weights, and it connects to equivariant architectures in scientific ML. The evidence comes from InceptionV1 plus some other image models.
items.takeaway: Many neurons are transformed versions of one feature, and the weights connecting them follow the same symmetry.

items.title: Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M)
items.why: A hands-on video that rebuilds a GPT-2 (124M) model step by step, suited to learning training and reproducibility details by working through code. The source page gave only the title and author, so its depth and its use of open code are not confirmed by the excerpt.

earlier.title: Why We Think
earlier.why: A structured review of test-time compute and chain-of-thought: latent-variable framing, parallel versus sequential search, RL for reasoning, and faithfulness. It gives useful context for judging reasoning-model claims.

earlier.title: Gradient-based Planning for World Models at Longer Horizons
earlier.why: A lab blog post on gradient-based planning through learned world models. It connects optimization conditioning with adversarial sensitivity of deep networks. It is useful for scientific-ML intuition about optimizing through learned simulators, but the evidence comes from the authors' own method and is not independently verified.
earlier.takeaway: The authors argue that action gradients are better behaved than state-input gradients, and build a planner that relies only on action Jacobians.
